title: Himself as subject
hookLine: I am myself the matter of my book, he tells the reader

cards: The first page of Montaigne's book doesn't invite you in. It tells you to stop reading. Before the first essay comes a short note headed To the reader.
It's a book of good faith, he says, written for his family and friends, so that after they lose him, they can find some trace of him again. Then the last lines: I am myself the matter of my book.
You'd be unreasonable, reader, to spend your free time on a subject so slight and so vain. So, farewell.

teach.b: First, who it was for. He had no thought of serving the reader, he says, or of his own glory. He wrote so the people who knew him could keep something of him after he died.
Second, how he wanted to be seen. If he'd wanted the world's favor, he'd have dressed himself up.
Instead he wants to be seen in his simple, natural, ordinary way, without strain or artifice, because it's himself he's painting. His faults will be there to read. Third, the subject.

teach.h: I AM THE MATTER OF MY BOOK.
teach.b: I am myself the matter of my book. Not kings, not wars, not the nature of the universe, though he touches all of those: one ordinary man, looked at honestly from the inside. Then the joke: why waste your time on that?
Farewell. Of course, the reader doesn't leave. Fourth, what writing himself did to him.
In a later essay he turns it around: I have no more made my book than my book has made me.
Painting himself for others, he says, he painted his inside in clearer colors than before. The writing changed the writer. You don't need to publish anything for that.
One honest paragraph about yourself, even one nobody reads, can show you to yourself in clearer colors.

how: Montaigne's Essays open with a short note to the reader saying the book was written for his family and friends, and that he himself is its subject, painted plainly, faults and all.

games.q: you're Montaigne, writing the note at the front of your book. if you wanted the world's favor, what would you do?
o: show your simple, ordinary self, faults included.
games.why: he says that if he'd wanted favor he'd have dressed up; instead he paints himself plainly, faults and all.

practice: Begin the way Montaigne might, simply, without dressing up: one thing you like, one thing you're bad at, one habit you'd rather nobody noticed, one thing you hope people remember. Say it to yourself plainly, not to impress anyone.

wordCard.voice: Himself as subject. Montaigne tells the reader, in his opening note, that he is himself the matter of his book, painted in his simple, ordinary way. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: myself the matter. The subject is always close at hand. Back tomorrow, same hill.
